weeks.topic: Closing WEEK 1: Introduction to Chemistry Definition, History, Branches, and Importance DEFINITION OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study of the composition, structure, properties, and changes (reactions) of matter. It seeks to understand:  What matter is made of (composition)  How matter is arranged (structure)  How matter behaves (properties)  How matter changes (chemical reactions) Chemistry is often called the "central science" because it connects and overlaps with other sciences like Physics, Biology, Medicine, and Geology. HISTORY OF CHEMISTRY The history of chemistry can be divided into several stages: a. Ancient Period (Before 16th Century)  Early humans used natural substances such as fire, salt, and metals like gold and copper without understanding their composition.  The practice of alchemy emerged, combining elements of magic, religion, and early experimentation.  Alchemists sought to transform base metals (like lead) into gold and to discover the elixir of life. b. Transition Period (16th-18th Century)  The idea of experimentation and observation started replacing mystical beliefs.  Robert Boyle (1627-1691) is regarded as the father of modern chemistry for his emphasis on experimentation and his famous Boyle's Law on gases.  Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794), called the father of modern chemistry, named "oxygen" and "hydrogen," and established the Law of Conservation of Mass. c. Modern Period (19th Century - Present)  Development of the Atomic Theory by John Dalton (1808).  Discovery of the Periodic Table by Dmitri Mendeleev (1869).  Advancements in physical chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry.  In the 20th century, chemistry expanded into nuclear chemistry, polymer chemistry, and analytical chemistry. BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry is broadly divided into the following branches: a. Physical Chemistry Deals with the physical properties and behavior of matter, energy changes, and reaction rates. Examples: study of thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, and kinetics. b. Organic Chemistry Study of compounds containing carbon (except carbonates and oxides of carbon). Examples: hydrocarbons, alcohols, and plastics. c. Inorganic Chemistry Study of elements and compounds that are not based on carbon. Examples: metals, salts, and minerals. d. Analytical Chemistry Focuses on methods used to determine the composition of substances (qualitative and quantitative analysis). Examples: titration, spectroscopy, chromatography. e. Biochemistry Study of chemical processes in living organisms. Examples: digestion, respiration, and photosynthesis. f. Industrial Chemistry Application of chemical principles in industries to produce useful materials such as fertilizers, paints, drugs, and soaps. IMPORTANCE OF CHEMISTRY Chemistry plays a vital role in everyday life and national development. a. In Medicine and Health  Production of drugs, vaccines, and anesthetics.  Development of disinfectants and diagnostic chemicals. b. In Agriculture  Manufacture of fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides.  Development of soil analysis and irrigation chemicals. c. In Industry  Production of plastics, paints, soap, cement, textiles, and cosmetics.  Extraction and purification of metals. d. In Environment  Helps to understand and control pollution.  Development of renewable energy sources. e. In Food and Nutrition  Preservation and processing of food.  Production of flavorings and supplements. f. In Scientific Research  Provides a foundation for innovations in energy, materials, and biotechnology. EVALUATION 1. Define chemistry and explain why it is called the "central science." 2. Outline the three main historical stages of chemistry and name one scientist associated with each stage. 3. Differentiate between organic and inorganic chemistry with examples. 4. Mention any four branches of chemistry and state one importance of each. 5. List five areas of human life where chemistry plays a major role. ASSIGNMENT 1. Write short notes on the contributions of Robert Boyle and Antoine Lavoisier to modern chemistry. 2. Make a neat diagram showing the major branches of chemistry. 3. Identify five industrial products made possible through chemistry and state their uses. WEEK 2 - CHEMICAL INDUSTRIES AND LABORATORY APPARATUS CHEMICAL INDUSTRIES Meaning of Chemical Industries Chemical industries are industries that use chemical substances at one stage or another to produce other chemicals or finished goods.  Raw materials: Substances used as starting materials in production.  Products: Finished goods from an industry, which may also serve as raw materials for another industry. Types of Raw Materials 1. Natural raw materials - Obtained directly from nature without major alteration. Examples: air, water, coal, limestone, petroleum, iron ore, sulphur deposits. 2. Synthetic raw materials - Man-made materials produced for further manufacturing. Examples: synthetic fibres, plastics, palm kernel oil for soaps, thread for textiles. Classification of Chemical Industries 1. Heavy Chemicals - Needed in large quantities; purity is not the top priority. Examples: tetraoxosulphate (VI) acid (H₂SO₄), sodium hydroxide, cement, palm kernel oil. 2. Fine Chemicals - Required in small quantities; produced in very pure form. Examples: sodium chloride (NaCl), dyes, preservatives, analytical reagents. Divisions According to Products  Glass industries - Use sand, clay, sodium carbonate, and colourants to make glass.  Ceramics industries - Use clay and fine chemicals to make ceramics.  Pharmaceutical industries - Use organic, inorganic, and synthetic chemicals to produce drugs.  Metallurgical industries - Extract and process metals from ores.  Fertilizer industries - Produce nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium compounds for agriculture.  Paint industries - Use pigments and inorganic chemicals to make paints. Importance of Chemical Industries  Provide raw materials for other industries.  Generate income and employment.  Serve as research centres and educational resources. Disadvantages of Chemical Industries  Cause environmental pollution.  Can lead to rural-urban migration.  Capital intensive to establish. WEEK 3 - NATURE OF MATTER - STATES, PROPERTIES, AND CHANGES OF STATE Meaning of Matter Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. All physical objects-whether visible (like a table) or invisible (like air)-are made of matter. Matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and molecules that are in constant motion. States of Matter Matter exists in three primary states: solid, liquid, and gas. In advanced science, two more states-plasma and Bose-Einstein condensate-are recognized, but at the secondary school level, we focus on the main three. (a) Solid  Particle arrangement: Particles are closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement.  Movement: Particles vibrate in fixed positions.  Shape and volume: Has a definite shape and definite volume.  Compressibility: Cannot be easily compressed due to little space between particles.  Examples: Wood, metal, stone, ice. (b) Liquid  Particle arrangement: Particles are close together but not in a fixed arrangement.  Movement: Particles can slide over each other, allowing liquids to flow.  Shape and volume: Has definite volume but no definite shape-it takes the shape of its container.  Compressibility: Almost incompressible.  Examples: Water, oil, alcohol, mercury. (c) Gas  Particle arrangement: Particles are far apart and not in a fixed position.  Movement: Move freely at high speed in all directions.  Shape and volume: Has neither definite shape nor definite volume-it expands to fill its container.  Compressibility: Highly compressible due to large spaces between particles.  Examples: Air, oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen. Properties of the States of Matter Property Solid Liquid Gas Shape Definite Indefinite Indefinite Volume Definite Definite Indefinite Arrangement of particles Fixed, closely packed Close, random Far apart, random Movement of particles Vibrate in place Slide over each other Move freely in all directions Density High Medium Low Compressibility Very low Very low High Energy of particles Lowest Moderate Highest Changes of State Changes of state occur when matter is transformed from one state to another by heating or cooling. These processes involve energy changes but do not alter the chemical composition of the substance. (a) Melting  Definition: Change from solid to liquid upon heating.  Example: Ice melting into water.  Energy change: Heat energy is absorbed to overcome the forces holding particles in fixed positions. (b) Freezing (Solidification)  Definition: Change from liquid to solid upon cooling.  Example: Water freezing into ice.  Energy change: Heat energy is released as particles slow down and become fixed. (c) Vaporization (Boiling/Evaporation)  Boiling: Rapid change from liquid to gas at a specific temperature (boiling point).  Evaporation: Slow change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature.  Example: Water boiling at 100°C; drying of wet clothes. (d) Condensation  Definition: Change from gas to liquid upon cooling.  Example: Water vapour forming droplets on a cold surface. (e) Sublimation  Definition: Direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.  Examples: Iodine crystals, dry ice (solid CO₂), naphthalene balls. (f) Deposition  Definition: Change from gas directly to solid without becoming liquid.  Example: Formation of frost. Particle Theory of Matter The Kinetic Theory of Matter explains that:

WEEK 4 - SEPARATION TECHNIQUES In chemistry, separation techniques are methods used to divide mixtures into their individual components, based on differences in physical or chemical properties such as particle size, density, solubility, boiling point, or magnetic properties. The choice of a suitable technique depends on:  The nature of the mixture (solid-solid, solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, gas mixtures).  The properties of the components.  The level of purity required. 1. Filtration  Definition: A process of separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a porous barrier (filter paper).  Principle: Based on particle size - solid particles are too large to pass through the filter pores.  Example: Separating sand from water. 2. Distillation  Definition: Separation of a liquid from a mixture using differences in boiling points.  Principle: Components with lower boiling points vaporize first, then condense back to liquid.  Example: Purifying water from saltwater.

Chromatography  Definition: Technique for separating components of a mixture based on their movement through a medium.  Principle: Components move at different rates due to differences in solubility and adsorption.  Example: Separating plant pigments on paper.

Decantation  Definition: Pouring off a liquid to separate it from sediment or an immiscible liquid.  Principle: Relies on density differences between substances.  Example: Removing water from settled sand. 8. Evaporation  Definition: Removal of a liquid by heating until only the solid residue remains.  Principle: Components with lower boiling points evaporate, leaving non-volatile solids behind.  Example: Obtaining salt from seawater. 9. Magnetic Separation  Definition: Use of magnets to separate magnetic materials from non-magnetic ones.  Principle: Based on magnetic properties of substances.  Example: Separating iron filings from sand.  Definition: Winnowing is a separation technique used to separate lighter particles (such as husks or chaff) from heavier particles (such as grains or seeds) using the action of wind or air currents.  Principle: The method works on the difference in weight (density) between the two substances - lighter materials are blown away by air, while heavier materials fall straight down.  Example: Separating paddy rice grains from husk after threshing. 11. Sieving  Definition: Sieving is a separation technique used to separate particles of different sizes by passing a mixture through a sieve or mesh that allows smaller particles to pass through while retaining the larger ones.  Principle: The method works based on the difference in particle size.  Example: Separating wheat flour from bran using a fine mesh sieve. 12. Sedimentation  Definition: Sedimentation is a separation technique in which insoluble, heavier particles in a liquid settle at the bottom under the influence of gravity.  Principle: The method is based on the difference in density between solid particles and the liquid.  Example: Allowing muddy water to stand so that sand and mud settle at the bottom. WEEK 6 - ATOMIC STRUCTURE - STRUCTURE OF THE ATOM, SUBATOMIC PARTICLES Meaning of Atom  An atom is the smallest particle of an element that takes part in chemical reactions and retains the chemical properties of that element.  Atoms are extremely small: e.g., radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m. Historical Development of the Atomic Model 1. Dalton's Atomic Theory (1803) o Atoms are indivisible, indestructible particles. o Atoms of the same element are identical; atoms of different elements differ. o Atoms combine in simple ratios to form compounds. o Limitation: Failed to explain subatomic particles and isotopes. 2. Thomson's Model (1897) - Plum pudding model o Discovered the electron. o Proposed that an atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded. o Limitation: Could not explain the stability of atoms. 3. Rutherford's Model (1911) - Nuclear model o Gold foil experiment showed atoms are mostly empty space. o Nucleus at the center, containing positive charges (protons). o Electrons revolve around nucleus like planets. o Limitation: Could not explain why electrons don't collapse into the nucleus. 4. Bohr's Model (1913) - Planetary model o Electrons revolve in fixed orbits (energy levels/shells). o Energy is absorbed or released when electrons jump between shells. o Limitation: Could not fully explain multi-electron atoms. 5. Modern Atomic Theory (Quantum Mechanical Model) o Developed by Schrödinger, Heisenberg, etc. o Electrons are in regions called orbitals, not fixed paths. o Atoms consist of a dense nucleus (protons + neutrons) with electrons in shells/subshells. Subatomic Particles Particle Symbol Charge Relative Mass Location in Atom Proton p⁺ +1 1 a.m.u. (≈1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) In nucleus Neutron n⁰ 0 1 a.m.u. (≈1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) In nucleus Electron e⁻ -1 1/1836 a.m.u. (≈9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) Orbiting nucleus in shells  Protons: Determine the identity of an element (Atomic number).  Neutrons: Provide stability in the nucleus.  Electrons: Involved in chemical bonding and reactions. Atomic Number and Mass Number  Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons in the nucleus.  Mass Number (A): Number of protons + neutrons.  Neutron number (N): N = A - Z. Example: Carbon-12 has Z = 6, A = 12 → Protons = 6, Neutrons = 6, Electrons = 6. Isotopes  Atoms of the same element (same Z) but different mass numbers (A).  Example: ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C are isotopes of carbon.  They have similar chemical properties but different physical properties. Atomic Structure Representation  Electrons are arranged in shells (K, L, M, N) according to the 2n² rule: o K shell → 2 electrons o L shell → 8 electrons o M shell → 18 electrons o N shell → 32 electrons Example:  Sodium (Z = 11) → 2, 8, 1  Oxygen (Z = 8) → 2, 6 EVALUATION 1. Define an atom. 2. State three limitations of Dalton's Atomic Theory. 3. Mention the scientist who discovered the electron. 4. Distinguish between atomic number and mass number. 5.
